To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

phytyl fatty esters (trans-phytol estersified with a fatty acids) are a new source for bioavailable phytanic acid (trans-phytanic acid) which has to be taken into account when calculating the tolerable daily intake for patients with Refsüm’s disease.
phytyl fatty acids in bell pepper are actually a source for bioactive trans-phytol, and that the consumption of bell pepper could lead to exploitation of tolerable daily intake.
phytyl esters of fatty acids (PFAE) in vegetables pose a health risk for Refsum patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of a new class of bioactive lipids, the PFAE, and their occurrence in food.
the identification of a new source of bioavailable trans- phytol in food.
a better understanding of the bioaccessibility and bioavailability of trans-phytol in PFAE and its relevance for patients suffering from the metabolic disorder Refsum’s disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bell pepper, rocket salad, and other vegetable matrices containing PFAE should be excluded from the diet of patients with Refsum's disease.
patients suffering from Refsus’ disease should not eat bell pepper and rocket salad.
patients with Refsum disease should avoid eating bell pepper and rocket salad.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the occurrence of PFAE in vegetables is an underestimated source of bioavailable trans- phytol for patients suffering from this disease.
PFAEs in vegetables should not be underestimated and should be considered in future risk assessments for patients suffering from this rare disease.
the intake of phytyl esters in vegetables should be avoided by patients suffering from Refsus’ disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the occurrence of trans-phytol in vegetables has been largely underestimated so far.
the presence of PFAE in foods should be taken into account in the future for the assessment of the risk for patients suffering form Refsum’s disease.
the presence of phytyl esters in vegetables should be considered when assessing the risk of phytanic and trans-phytanic acid accumulation in humans with Refsum’s Disease.
